title_extracted: Finite Element Analysis of Second-Order Strain-Gradient Elasticity with                     Ellipsoidal Nonlocal Characteristic Lengths              Vipin Gupta1, Sunita Kumawat2, Arun Kumar Yadav3, Taizo Maruyama4, Bandar Almohsen5,∗
abstract:
This study presents an anisotropic strain-gradient elasticity framework in which direction-dependent microstructural in-

teractions arise from a geometrically defined nonlocal domain. The resulting characteristic-length tensor comes from the

second moments of a three-dimensional ellipsoidal averaging domain, giving it a direct geometric meaning similar to a
fabric tensor. A positive-definite strain-gradient energy is discretized using smooth, continuously differentiable Hermite

finite elements in one, two, and three dimensions, together with a corrected consistent mass formulation. For an axial char-

acteristic length of 0.20 m and transverse lengths of 0.02 m, rotating the microstructural orientation produces a monotonic

response. Static displacement increases by about 4%, while the fundamental frequency decreases from 186.3 Hz to 173.1

Hz. The normalised frequency ranges from 1.054 to 0.979 relative to a volume-equivalent isotropic reference of 177.0 Hz.
The axial length dominates the transverse contribution, producing a 5.8% stiffness increase compared with only 0.5% in
the transverse-dominant case. A Directional Stiffening Index, measured against a volume-equivalent isotropic reference,

is predominantly positive, ranging from 0% to about 30% across the anisotropy ratios and orientations studied. Only a
few high-angle configurations show small negative values. These trends allow the stiffness and vibration frequency of

anisotropic microstructured materials to be tailored through controlled variation of characteristic length and orientation.

8. Conclusion

 A three-dimensional computational framework for second-order strain-gradient elasticity was developed based on an
ellipsoidal nonlocal averaging neighbourhood. A C1-continuous tensor-product tricubic Hermite finite element formula-

tion solved the highly coupled fourth-order anisotropic governing equations while satisfying the continuity requirements

imposed by strain-gradient theory. The central new phenomenon identified in this work is orientation-induced mono-

tonic tuning. Unlike axis-aligned models, where f1 has no orientation dependence, the rotated model shows monotonic
decrease. This arises from competition between the slope constraint with clamped-gradient ui, j = 0 and the curvature
penalty 1/20LmnCε,mε,n. Boundary layer thickness a = √︁ l2/10 competes with structural length L. For lx ≫ly, large L11
at 0◦penalizes axial curvature strongly and increases stiffness. At 45◦the off-diagonal L12 transfers energy to transverse
gradients, reducing axial penalty and causing frequency drop. Axial dominance has a clear physical reason. Primary
strain εxx has gradient ∂εxx/∂x localized in the boundary layer near x = 0 and weighted by l2x. Transverse gradients ∂ε/∂y
remain small due to slender Ly/Lx = 0.2 and uniform traction. Hence ly contributes 0.5% while lx contributes 5.8%. Field-
level confirmation via contours in Fig.7 and Fig.9 shows smooth monotonic |u| with more gradual near-edge rise for large
lx, confined to a/L ≈0.016. Engineering implication is that three design regions in Fig.11 enable tailoring. These are
stiffening-optimal for maximum stiffness, frequency-tuning for vibration isolation without stiffness loss, and insensitive

for robust design. The implementation stayed numerically stable across the full parameter space: the estimated condition
number rose only moderately and stayed below the order of 106 even for the most demanding anisotropic configurations.
It picked up the combined effects of microstructural elongation and rotational alignment on both the static and dynamic

responses of gradient elastic solids.

  The principal findings of the present study are summarized as follows:

   • A unified bivariate surface-based framework was proposed to evaluate how the anisotropy ratio (AR) and orientation
      angle (θ) act together.  Unlike conventional one-parameter investigations, this approach brings out the coupled

      interaction between characteristic-length anisotropy and orientation, giving a fuller picture of directional strain-
      gradient stiffening.

   • A new Directional Stiffening Index (DSI) was introduced to put a number on the percentage reduction in displace-

     ment relative to a volume-equivalent isotropic reference configuration. The index gives a physically meaningful
     way to turn abstract characteristic-length tensors into practical structural stiffening performance.

   • The static response shows maximum strain-gradient stiffening for the axially aligned configuration (AR = 20, θ =
       0◦), where the normalised displacement ratio hits its minimum value. The gradient enrichment becomes weak, on
      the other hand, for nearly isotropic characteristic-length distributions and for orientations approaching θ = 90◦.

   • The dynamic response shows monotonic decrease similar to static but governed by modal stiffness. The highest
      normalised fundamental frequency occurs at (AR = 20, θ = 0◦), and frequency decreases monotonically to 173.06
    Hz at 90◦.

   • Throughout the parameter space we looked at, the tricubic Hermite formulation stayed computationally robust.

     Even for the strongest anisotropic configurations, the estimated condition number stayed within a numerically

       stability and reliability of the numerical implementation.

  From an engineering standpoint, the framework gives a quantitative way to tailor the stiffness and dynamic response of

microstructured materials with directional internal architectures, including fibre-reinforced composites, lattice metama-
terials, and additively manufactured structures. The orientation-based design maps and the Directional Stiffening Index

work as practical tools for picking characteristic-length configurations that maximise structural performance. Future work

will extend the formulation to coupled multiphysics problems involving thermoelastic, piezoelectric, and piezomagnetic

gradient continua, along with transient wave propagation and dispersion analyses in strongly anisotropic microstructured

materials.

abstract:
This paper develops a displacement-based finite element framework for Mindlin Form-II strain-
gradient elasticity and uses it to study anisotropic size-dependent behavior. The formulation
combines a C1-continuous Bogner–Fox–Schmit (BFS) element with an orientation-dependent
characteristic-length tensor derived from a three-dimensional ellipsoidal microstructure, and
captures the combined effect of microstructural aspect ratio and orientation under simple
shear.  Accuracy is checked against a closed-form analytical benchmark.  Parametric analy-
ses over aspect ratio and orientation angle then examine the displacement field, Cauchy stress,
higher-order double stress, boundary-layer thickness, and strain-gradient energy. Both param-
eters strongly affect the non-classical response: higher-order stresses rise and boundary layers
thicken with increasing anisotropy.  Three-dimensional response surfaces, design maps, and
energy-partition diagrams trace the transition from classical elasticity to gradient-dominated
behavior and show mechanical energy shifting from the classical strain field into the higher-order
gradient term. The framework is suited to architected and cellular materials with anisotropic
microstructures, and to size-dependent analysis of composites, lattice materials, and MEMS
components.

6. Conclusions

  This work combined Mindlin Form-II strain-gradient elasticity with a C1-continuous Bogner–
Fox–Schmit finite element formulation to study how anisotropic ellipsoidal microstructures
affect the response of size-dependent solids under simple shear. The model uses an orientation-
dependent characteristic-length tensor, which lets the microstructural aspect ratio and orien-
tation be varied independently. The implementation was first checked against an established
analytical benchmark, with close quantitative agreement. The main findings follow.

   • The BFS formulation reproduces the analytical benchmark solution and retains the con-
     tinuous second-order derivatives that strain-gradient elasticity requires. It ran stably over
     the full parameter range without artificial stabilization.

   • Increasing the orientation angle α raises the boundary-normal characteristic length g222(α).
     Aligning the ellipsoid with the boundary normal strengthens the higher-order non-local in-
      teractions, produces larger double shear stresses, and thickens the strain-gradient bound-
     ary layers at the constrained interfaces.

   • The aspect ratio controls the spatial distribution of the higher-order internal forces.
     Highly elongated microstructures concentrate stress at the boundaries and amplify the
      non-classical effects throughout the domain.

   • The three-dimensional response surfaces and design maps trace the transition from clas-
       sical Cauchy elasticity to gradient-dominated behaviour, showing how aspect ratio and
      orientation act together.

title_extracted: A Total-Lagrangian C1 Bogner–Fox–Schmit Formulation for     Finite-Strain Mindlin Form-II Strain-Gradient Elasticity
abstract:
A displacement-based total-Lagrangian finite element formulation is developed for geo-
metrically nonlinear Mindlin Form-II strain-gradient elasticity. The formulation employs
the Green–Lagrange strain and its material gradient as constitutive variables together
with a Saint–Venant–Kirchhoff hyperelastic model and an isotropic sixth-order Mindlin
strain-gradient constitutive law. A bicubic C1 Bogner–Fox–Schmit finite element satisfies
the continuity requirements of the displacement-only weak form, and an exact consistent
tangent matrix yields quadratic convergence in the Newton–Raphson solver. The for-
mulation is verified against the Shekarchizadeh et al.  [1] two-dimensional simple-shear
benchmark, recovering the analytical displacement profiles with observed convergence
rates close to four in L2, three in H1, and two in the strain-gradient measure. Cantilever
bending is then analyzed under finite deformation to assess mesh convergence, inter-
nal length-scale effects, higher-order boundary conditions, and the sensitivity to the five
isotropic Mindlin constants. The results show that strain-gradient contributions increase
apparent cantilever stiffness by roughly 5%, reduce tip displacement by approximately
4.3–4.7%, and regularize localized strain concentrations near the clamped boundary. The
formulation provides a displacement-only finite element framework for Mindlin Form-II
strain-gradient elasticity undergoing finite deformation, operating entirely on a single
primal displacement field.

9. Conclusions

   This work developed a displacement-based total-Lagrangian finite element formulation
for geometrically nonlinear Mindlin Form-II strain-gradient elasticity under plane-strain
conditions. The mechanical response was formulated using the Green–Lagrange strain
and its material gradient, combining a Saint–Venant–Kirchhoff hyperelastic potential
with an isotropic sixth-order Mindlin gradient energy, discretized via a C1 Bogner–Fox–
Schmit rectangular element.
   The main findings are as follows:

   • The exact consistent linearization of the finite-strain residual yields classical mate-
       rial, classical geometric, gradient material, and gradient geometric tangent contri-
      butions, enabling quadratic convergence in a displacement-only Newton–Raphson
      solver.

   • The analytical Shekarchizadeh–Abali–Bersani benchmark was recovered in the in-
      finitesimal regime for both displacement- and traction-controlled cases. The ob-
     served mesh-convergence rates were close to four in the displacement L2 measure,
      three in the H1 measure, and two in the strain-gradient measure.

   • The finite-strain mesh study showed monotonic convergence of tip displacement
     and internal energy for both the classical and gradient-enhanced materials. The
      refined 64 × 16 mesh served as the numerical reference for the mesh-convergence
      assessment.

   • Increasing the internal length scale enhances apparent structural stiffness and sup-
      presses local strain-gradient intensity.  At ℓ/H = 0.1, the apparent stiffness is
     approximately 5% above the classical baseline, while the maximum strain-gradient
     measure decreases to approximately 0.19 of its classical reference value.

   • Under finite end-shear loading, the tip displacement decreased from 0.6043H in the
      classical case to 0.5761H for ℓ/H = 0.1. Full-field contours confirm that the primary
     bending and shear distributions are preserved, while localized strain gradients are
      regularized near the clamped support.

   • The local strain-gradient response was most sensitive to a5, followed by a1, whereas
     the global stiffness, tip displacement, and stored energy were only weakly affected
     by one-at-a-time changes in the individual gradient constants.

   • Higher-order boundary conditions noticeably influence both the localized strain-
      gradient field and the overall structural compliance. Releasing the normal slope and
      enforcing zero natural double traction increased the finite-load tip displacement by
     approximately 3.6% and produced a twofold increase in the peak strain-gradient
      intensity. In addition, the strain-gradient energy fraction rose systematically from
      zero in the classical case to approximately 1.3% and 2.3% at ℓ/H = 0.05 and 0.1,
      respectively.

   The formulation is directly applicable to parametric studies of rectangular plane-strain
strips and cantilever members in which a support or loaded edge produces localized strain-
gradient concentrations. In such problems, it provides a computational tool to evaluate
the influence of the internal length scale and the choice of higher-order boundary data.

abstract:
Flexoelectricity couples electric polarization to strain gradients and, unlike piezoelectricity, is
      permitted by symmetry in every dielectric, so it becomes a candidate transduction mechanism pre-
       cisely at sub-micrometre scales. The governing equations of a coupled piezoelectric–flexoelectric
       solid with Mindlin Form-II strain-gradient elasticity form a fourth-order electromechanical sys-
     tem whose conforming discretization requires C1 continuity and whose raw stiffness matrix spans
     some twenty orders of magnitude. This paper develops a conforming Bogner–Fox–Schmit finite
      element formulation for this coupled problem in plane strain, adopting a shear-free flexoelectric
       specialization and applying a complete non-dimensionalization as a symmetric congruence that
      improves the conditioning by more than twenty orders of magnitude without altering the physical
      solution. The two-mesh rates computed from the source-reported Shekarchizadeh norms are
      3.9998, 2.9963 and 1.9995, consistent with the theoretical orders 4, 3 and 2; the adopted PZT-5H
      constants reproduce the IEEE Std 176 analytical chain (k31 = 0.3887 against the tabulated 0.39,
      Eopen = 71.38 GPa, Timoshenko tip deflection 5.65×10−14 m) and the electromechanical energy
       identities to a relative residual of order 10−12. Studies of a barium titanate cantilever reveal a
       self-stiffening saturation of the open-circuit potential, a critical thickness scaling hcrit ∝ℓ0.90
      obtained by an empirical power-law fit to four source-reported critical-thickness roots, and an
      energy conversion ratio that decreases with slenderness in the reduced model, traced to the
      absence of the transverse bending coupling rather than to any computational defect. The results
      delineate which size-dependent responses the shear-free model captures and which require the
        full flexoelectric tensor.

conclusion_excerpt:
6  Conclusions

A conforming C1 Bogner–Fox–Schmit finite element formulation has been developed for coupled
piezoelectric–flexoelectric solids with Mindlin Form-II strain-gradient elasticity in plane strain.
The formulation spans the complete chain from the electric enthalpy and the five Mindlin–Eshel
invariants to the explicit fourth-order electromechanical strong form, the boundary operators
including the double traction and corner forces, and the symmetric indefinite saddle system of the
discretisation.

   The constitutive model adopts a reduced flexoelectric specialization in which the shear coefficient
is set to zero, following the established practice for barium titanate benchmarks, and states this
specialization explicitly. The discretisation uses the bicubic Hermite interpolation of the BFS
element, which provides exactly the C1 continuity demanded by the fourth-order mechanical
operators, with 4 × 4 Gauss–Legendre integration that is exact for every integrand.
  A complete non-dimensionalization of the field variables, applied as a symmetric congruence
transformation, reduces the condition number of the constrained coupled system by more than
twenty orders of magnitude on slender meshes while leaving the physical solution invariant to
within a relative residual of 3.5 × 10−13. The energy bookkeeping distinguishes the dead-load
product P = 2Uint from the quasi-static work Wqs = 12P, and the conversion ratio is defined on the
dead-load product consistently.
   The two-mesh rates computed from the source-reported Shekarchizadeh norms are 3.9998, 2.9963
and 1.9995, consistent with the theoretical orders of the bicubic element; the adopted PZT-5H
constants reproduce the IEEE Std 176 analytical chain (k31 = 0.3887 against the tabulated 0.39,
Eopen = 71.38 GPa, tip deflection 5.65 × 10−14 m) and the electromechanical energy identities to a
relative residual of order 10−12.

   The size-dependent response of the barium titanate cantilever exhibits a self-stiffening saturation
of the open-circuit potential at Λ of order 10−2; the rise–maximum–fall non-monotonicity persists
under through-thickness refinement from 16 × 2 to 60 × 12 elements, while the quantitative peak
values carry the resolution caveats of Section 4.8. The same studies yield a near-linear critical-
thickness law hcrit ≈24 ℓfitted to four source-reported roots, and an energy conversion ratio that
decreases with slenderness in the reduced model. The last observation is traced to the absence of
the transverse bending polarization in the shear-free specialization, and it demarcates the physical
regime in which the full flexoelectric tensor is required.

   The practical significance of the work is twofold. For device analysis, the formulation provides a

verified and numerically tractable computational basis for piezoelectric–flexoelectric cantilever and
plate problems, with the critical thickness law supplying a direct design rule. For model selection,
the work quantifies precisely which size-dependent phenomena are captured by the shear-free limit
and which are not, so that the constitutive specialization can be chosen deliberately rather than
implicitly.

  A natural extension is the incorporation of the full three-parameter isotropic flexoelectric tensor,
for which the discretisation, the conditioning treatment, and the energy machinery developed here
carry over unchanged. The diagnostic transverse-coupling study reported in this work already

abstract:
Pyroelectric crystals are necessarily also piezoelectric, so a spatially non-uniform temper-
      ature field drives both a direct pyroelectric response and an indirect piezoelectric response
     mediated by thermal strain. We present a variational finite-element model, based on a single
      electric-enthalpy potential and a conforming C1 Bogner–Fox–Schmit element, for the open-
       circuit voltage of a plane-strain tetragonal BaTiO3 microcantilever under a steady through-
      thickness temperature difference. For a tetragonal crystal, the plane-strain thermal-stress vec-
      tor must be obtained by contracting the full three-dimensional thermal-expansion and elastic
      tensors before the plane-strain constraint is imposed; a simplified reduction that omits the con-
      strained transverse thermal expansion under-predicts the resulting thermal-stress components
     by 35–58% and, for the present geometry and loading, reverses the sign of the piezoelectric-
      thermal contribution to the open-circuit voltage. We also distinguish the fixed-strain (primary)
      pyroelectric coefficient required by the strain-based constitutive law from the free (total) co-
       efficient ordinarily reported from bulk measurements, taking the primary coefficient from a
       first-principles calculation and the anisotropic thermal-expansion coefficients from regression
       of single-crystal diffraction data. On a mesh-converged discretization, the pyroelectric-only,
       piezoelectric-plus-pyroelectric, and piezoelectric-plus-thermal open-circuit voltages are approx-
      imately −3.4 V, −1.5 V, and +0.19 V for a 10 µm × 1 µm specimen under a 10 K temperature
       difference. The polarity of the piezoelectric-thermal voltage is robust to the propagated un-
      certainty of the thermal-expansion regression at one standard deviation, reversing only beyond
      approximately two standard deviations on the transverse coefficient, while the pyroelectric-only
      voltage is sensitive to the uncertain clamped-versus-free classification of the transverse dielectric
      constant. We did not identify an experimental full-device voltage measurement for direct com-
      parison. An optional flexoelectric extension is retained in the formulation but excluded from
      the quantitative results, since neither an effective flexoelectric tensor nor an internal length
       scale is presently available for this material.

abstract:
The Guyer–Krumhansl equation models room-temperature heat conduction in heteroge-
neous media with three coefficients – diffusivity α, flux relaxation time τq and nonlocal
coefficient κ2 – routinely obtained by fitting heat pulse experiments.  Its solutions co-
incide with Fourier solutions at B = κ2/(ατq) = 1; this cancellation is established, but
its consequence for coefficient recoverability has not been quantified in the literature
considered here. This study analyses the rear-face parameter-to-observable map using
Fisher information, profile likelihood, Monte Carlo recovery and Bayesian model selection.
At B = 1 the response is independent of τq for any position, time or excitation, with
∂T/∂τq = −α ∂T/∂κ2 exactly; the Fisher matrix is singular and (τq, κ2) is structurally
non-identifiable. Away from resonance the degeneracy broadens into a configuration-
dependent band, B ∈[0.628, 1.804] at a 20% standard-error criterion; at B = 1 specifically
the Bayesian information criterion selects the Fourier model over Guyer–Krumhansl even
for Guyer–Krumhansl data, while α and B remain determined to 1% and 4–10%: the
degeneracy affects the (τq, κ2) split alone. Of twelve audited published calibrations, eight
lie inside the band and eleven report no uncertainty; two published evaluations of the
same basalt specimens differ in τq by factors of 1.51–3.50; the refined evaluation reports
R2 > 0.99. The forward operator was validated against three published reference figures
without fitting, at normalised errors of 0.384%, 0.382% and 0.483%. Guyer–Krumhansl
estimates are best reported in the (α, B) parameterisation, and campaigns targeting
τq should be designed away from resonance. No experimental validation of the inverse
conclusions is claimed.

13. Conclusions

   The parameter-to-observable map of the one-dimensional Guyer–Krumhansl heat pulse
problem has been analysed as an inverse problem, using a Laplace-domain convolution solver
with analytic sensitivities, cross-checked against an independent finite-difference scheme


                                      37

--- PAGE 38 ---
and an arbitrary-precision reference, and externally validated against three published
figures of an independently authored analytical solution at normalised errors of 0.384%,
0.382% and 0.483% with no parameter fitting.
   Three findings follow. First, at the Fourier resonance B = κ2/(ατq) = 1, a condition
established in the existing literature and not claimed here, the response is independent of
the relaxation time at every position and time and for any excitation; the sensitivities satisfy
∂T/∂τq = −α ∂T/∂κ2 exactly, so the sensitivity matrix has rank one with null direction
(1, α), the Fisher matrix is singular, and τq and κ2 are structurally non-identifiable from
any temperature record at any noise level or sampling density. Second, the degeneracy
is not confined to that point:  for the tested configuration the relaxation time carries
a standard error above 20% throughout B ∈[0.628, 1.804] and above 50% throughout
B ∈[0.817, 1.252]; at B = 1 specifically, within this ill-conditioned region, the Bayesian
information criterion selects the Fourier model over the Guyer–Krumhansl model even
for Guyer–Krumhansl data, while away from resonance the Guyer–Krumhansl model is
selected decisively at every tested condition, including B = 1.28 inside the 20% band.
Third, the record nevertheless remains informative: the diffusivity is recovered to about
1% and the resonance number to between 4% and 10% across the whole range including
exactly at resonance, so what fails is the resolution of a determined combination into two
coefficients rather than the determination of the transport behaviour.
   The contribution is therefore a statement about estimation rather than constitutive
modelling: a coincidence already known at the level of solutions is shown to impose
an exact rank deficiency on the inverse problem, with the neighbourhood in which that
deficiency dominates finite-noise estimation quantified. The practical consequence is
concrete: of twelve audited published calibrations, eight lie inside the band and eleven
report no parameter uncertainty, and two independent evaluations of the same three basalt
specimens return relaxation times differing by factors of 1.51 to 3.50, with the refined
evaluation reporting R2 > 0.99; this is consistent with, though not attributable solely to,
the identified structure. Guyer–Krumhansl coefficients are best reported in the (α, B)
parameterisation, and campaigns targeting the relaxation time should select specimens
away from resonance, since specimen thickness leaves B invariant.
   The analysis is confined to the one-dimensional slab and to synthetic inverse experiments;
the band boundaries are properties of the stated observation design and only the singularity
at their centre is universal. No experimental validation of the inverse conclusions is
claimed. The most useful extension is a controlled heat pulse experiment on a specimen of
independently determined B, which would test the predicted precision directly and, for
a specimen placed away from resonance, establish whether the relaxation and nonlocal
coefficients can be separated in practice at the precision the present analysis predicts.

abstract:
Surface-wave propagation in a two-dimensional (2D) hexagonal quasicrystal half-space is anal-
    ysed within a linear piezoelectric–thermoelastic formulation that treats the phonon and phason
    degrees of freedom on equal footing. The active sagittal problem couples the phonon displace-
   ments (ux, uz), the phason displacements (wx, wz), and the temperature increment θ; in the
    studied configuration (propagation along a two-fold axis, periodic direction inert) the electric
    potential decouples exactly and enters only as a passive output. Three phason dynamic models
    are compared: an inertial model (A, ρw ¨w = div H), a diffusive model (B, Dw ˙w = div H),
   and a telegraph-type model (C, ρw ¨w + Dw ˙w = div H), with Lord–Shulman thermal relax-
    ation. The surface-wave problem is reduced, without spatial discretisation of the half-space,
    to a 5 × 5 boundary matrix B(ω, k) assembled from the five decaying depth roots of a tenth-
    degree matrix pencil M(ω, k, p) = A0 +pA1 +p2A2; the secular condition is monitored through
    the scale-explicit indicator r = σmin(B)/∥B∥. After verification against classical elastic limits,
    symbolic identities, and the model limits C→A and C→B, the production sweeps show: (i) at
    baseline friction the phason-dominated branch of model A (V ∗≈0.3107, phason participa-
    tion Pw ≈0.99) is separated by ∆AC ≈0.33 from the phonon–Rayleigh branches of models
  B and C (V ∗≈0.4663), whereas B and C are mutually indistinguishable over 95 of 121 grid
    points within a benchmarked numerical-resolution floor ε∆= 1.13×10−8; (ii) when the phason
    friction D∗w is controlled, the B–C difference becomes resolvable (up to 5.0 × 10−3 relative) in
    a region of the (Ω, D∗w) plane that slides with D∗w, while at the baseline D∗w the two models
    remain indistinguishable almost everywhere; (iii) thermal relaxation (sweep in τ0∗ ) produces a
   weak but resolvable effect, max ∆T = 7.9 × 10−5, at the largest relaxation time; (iv) clamping
    the phason at the surface changes the model-C wave speed by at most 8.1 × 10−6 relative, and
    destroys the model-A surface branch altogether. Physically, the results indicate that the pha-
    son dynamic class controls which surface branch exists — inertial phasons carry a distinct slow
    surface mode, whereas dissipative phasons are slaved to the phonon–Rayleigh branch — while
    the diffusive/telegraph distinction is observable only when the phason friction is low (or the
    frequency high) relative to the phason inertia. The findings are statements about the declared
    composite/surrogate parameter set, bounded by the numerical resolution floor; no experimen-
     tal validation is claimed, and no claim beyond the investigated parameter ranges is made.
    All computations are nondimensional, deterministic, and reproducible from the accompanying
    reproducibility package.

8  Conclusions

   1. Formulation. A complete semi-analytical surface-wave formulation for 2D hexagonal piezo-
      electric thermoelastic quasicrystals (Laue class 10) has been established and verified. Physical
     meaning: the sagittal problem is a five-field boundary-value problem whose depth structure
       is a tenth-degree matrix pencil preserving the phason-stress asymmetry Hxz̸ = Hzx. Mod-
      elling implication:  the formulation provides an exact, discretisation-free baseline against
     which layered, graded, or discretised treatments of this material class can be checked.

   2. Verification.  Classical limits are reproduced to machine precision (vP /v0 = 1, vS/v0 =
      1/2; Rayleigh ratio to 1.1 × 10−11), symbolic identities hold exactly, and the model limits
   C→A and C→B are verified on the full grid (≤3.3 × 10−9) with branch-identity-verified
      continuation.  Physical meaning: model C genuinely interpolates between the inertial and
      diffusive classes; the retained 10−8 evidence curve quantifies the smooth non-uniformity of
     the singular Dw →0 limit below Ω≈0.32. Modelling implication: telegraph-type phason
     models can be used safely as one-parameter families, with the limit statements carrying their
      verified Ωranges.

     model A supports a phason-dominated branch at V ∗≈0.311 (Pw ≈0.99), while models B
     and C both support the phonon–Rayleigh branch at V ∗≈0.466, mutually indistinguishable
      over 95/121 grid points within the benchmarked floor. Physical meaning:  inertial phasons
      carry their own surface mode; dissipative phasons are slaved to the phonon field. Modelling
      implication: the choice of phason dynamic law is a branch-selection decision that must be
    made before quantitative work; diffusive versus telegraph is not such a decision at baseline
       friction.

    ≤1.25 × 10−7 across the map. The operator crossover Ωc = D∗w/ρ∗w is a reference line; no

abstract:
This investigation develops a theoretical and numerical analysis of torsional surface elastic waves
  propagating along a bounded three-layer cylindrical acoustic waveguide. The composite structure
   consists of an inner isotropic thermoelastic core (r < a), an intermediate conventional elastic
  cladding (a < r < b), and an outer finite-thickness elastic metamaterial shell (b < r < c)
  governed by a frequency-dependent dynamic shear compliance following Drude’s local-resonance
  model, s(3)44 (ω) = s0(1 −ω2p/ω2). The outermost boundary (r = c) is endowed with intrin-
   sic surface elasticity and residual surface tension formulated within the continuum framework
   of Gurtin and Murdoch. Imperfect bonding at the concentric interfaces r = a and r = b is
  incorporated via azimuthal linear shear spring compliance parameters ka and kb. The dynamic
  formulation is developed in cylindrical coordinates, retaining both modified Bessel functions of
  the first and second kinds (I1, K1) within the finite metamaterial shell. We provide an exact
   analytical proof demonstrating that because pure axisymmetric torsional wave motion is strictly
   isochoric (volumetric dilatation e ≡∇· u = 0), the thermal field is identically decoupled
  from the mechanical equation of motion and boundary tractions within the idealized linear
   isotropic formulation; consequently, the dispersion relation is completely independent of thermal
   conductivity, specific heat, and thermal relaxation parameters. The exact 5 × 5 characteris-
   tic dispersion determinant det M(ξ, Ω) = 0 is solved using a predictor–corrector continuation
   root-tracking algorithm cross-verified against high-density global bracket scans. For the base-
   line parameter set, the fundamental surface-wave branch exists inside the negative-compliance
  regime (Ω≤0.1709 ≪Ωp ≈2.0), producing an extreme phase-velocity reduction down
   to vp = 29.87 m/s (37 times slower than the bulk shear speed of the intermediate layer)
  and backward-wave intervals characterized by negative group velocity in the resonance/plateau
   region. An objective, grid-independent localization metric based on interface amplitude ratios
   reveals a modal transition: under baseline sub-millimeter-scale surface elasticity, the wave dis-
  placement maximum migrates from the outer boundary (r = c) to the internal spring interface
  (r = b) above a crossover wavenumber ξtrans ≈1.50 (dynamically computed ξtrans = 1.496);
   conversely, an engineered surface coating with O(1) dimensionless surface elasticity anchors the
  modal displacement toward the outer boundary over the investigated portion of the physical
  branch. The numerical solver is verified against published literature benchmarks for a reduced
  two-medium cylindrical problem (Kiełczyński et al., Sensors 25:143, 2025), reproducing the pub-
   lished tabulated wavenumbers and phase velocities within 0.02%, with the reported cylindrical
   cutoff frequency also recovered consistently, and against planar surface-plasmon-polariton limits.
   Finally, a quantitative sensitivity framework is established, delineating the operational limits for
   potential mass and acoustic viscosity sensor designs.

13 Conclusions

This study established an elastodynamic formulation and systematic numerical investigation of tor-
sional surface elastic waves propagating in a bounded three-layer cylindrical waveguide comprising
an isotropic thermoelastic core, an intermediate conventional elastic layer, and an outer Drude meta-
material shell with Gurtin–Murdoch surface elasticity and imperfect spring interfaces. The principal
findings are:

1. Exact Thermoelastic Decoupling: Pure axisymmetric torsional wave motion is proven to be
   strictly isochoric (e ≡∇·u = 0). Consequently, thermal expansion terms vanish from shear stresses,
  and the thermo-mechanical coupling term vanishes from the generalized heat conduction equation.
  The dispersion relation det M(ξ, Ω) = 0 is completely independent of thermal conductivity, specific
   heat, and thermal relaxation time within the linear model.
2. Negative-Compliance Guidance: Evanescent torsional surface waves exist below the Drude
   metamaterial resonance frequency (Ω≤0.1709 ≪Ωp ≈2.0 for baseline parameters), where
  dynamic compliance is negative (s(3)44 < 0).
3. Subwavelength Velocity Reduction and Backward Waves: The fundamental mode exhibits
   phase-velocity reduction down to vp =  29.87 m/s (37 times slower than the bulk shear
   speed in PMMA) and backward-wave intervals characterized by negative group velocity in the
   resonance/plateau region.
4. Modal Localization Transition: Under baseline sub-millimeter-scale surface elasticity, the wave
   displacement maximum migrates from the outer boundary (r = c) to the internal compliant
   interface (r = b) above ξtrans ≈1.50 (ξtrans = 1.496). However, an engineered surface coating with
   µ∗s ∼O(1) anchors the modal displacement to the outer boundary across the investigated portion
   of the physical branch, from its modal onset to ξ = 6.
5. Asymmetric Interface Sensitivity: Imperfect bonding at the outer metamaterial interface (k∗b)
   strongly modulates the plateau frequency (209.8% shift), whereas core interface bonding (k∗a) has
   negligible influence on the plateau.
6. Independent Literature Verification: The numerical solver was verified against published
   literature for a reduced two-medium cylindrical problem [47], reproducing the published tabulated
  wavenumbers and phase velocities within 0.02%, with the reported cylindrical cutoff frequency
   also recovered consistently, and asymptotically recovering the planar SPP limit.
